title: Signal Processing for Scientists (DSP)
subject: Signal Processing
summary: Twenty short lessons on the signal processing behind every digital instrument: sampling, aliasing and ADC bit depth; convolution and LTI systems; the DFT/FFT with its resolution, zero-padding and windowing traps; FIR and IIR filters, moving-average and Savitzky-Golay smoothing, and a light z-transform; noise, averaging and lock-in detection; and then the applications a chemist already uses: FT-NMR (FID, apodisation, phase correction), FT-IR (interferogram), deconvolution, baseline correction and peak picking. Concept first; calculation is a minority of the work.

units.title: Sampling and Digitisation
units.summary: How a continuous voltage becomes a list of numbers and what is lost: the sampling theorem, aliasing (folded peaks, mains hum) and quantisation (ADC bit depth and dynamic range in NMR receivers and detectors).

lessons.title: Signals, Sampling and Digitising: the Big Picture
objectives: Distinguish a continuous signal x(t), a sampled sequence x[n]=x(nT_s) and a digitised (quantised) sequence, naming the instrument stage that produces each.
Convert between sampling interval, sampling rate and record length, e.g. NMR dwell time and number of points to acquisition time.

lessons.title: The Sampling Theorem and the Nyquist Frequency
objectives: State the sampling theorem and explain, using the picture of spectral copies repeating every f_s, why f_s > 2 f_max is needed.
Compute the minimum sampling rate and Nyquist frequency for a given bandwidth.
Explain why ideal (sinc) reconstruction recovers a band-limited signal, and why real systems sample well above 2 f_max.

lessons.title: Aliasing in Practice: Folded Peaks, Hum and Anti-Alias Filters
objectives: Predict the apparent frequency of a tone above the Nyquist frequency.
Explain why aliasing cannot be removed after digitising and why an analogue anti-alias filter (or oversampling plus digital filtering) comes first.
Recognise aliasing in instrument data: mains hum, folded peaks in a too-narrow spectral width, stroboscopic effects.

lessons.title: Quantisation, ADC Bit Depth and Dynamic Range
objectives: Explain quantisation error as noise of RMS Δ/√12, where Δ is one least-significant bit, and use SQNR ≈ 6.02N + 1.76 dB.
Choose a bit depth for a required dynamic range and explain why a huge peak (solvent line, major isotope) limits what weak signals a digitiser can see.

units.title: Linear Systems and the Fourier Transform
units.summary: LTI systems and convolution (instrument response, line broadening), then the DFT and FFT: what a frequency bin means, why resolution is 1/T, what zero-padding does not do, how windowing controls leakage, and the convolution theorem with deconvolution.

lessons.title: Linear Time-Invariant Systems and the Impulse Response
objectives: Test whether a simple system (square-law detector, moving average, running difference) is linear and time-invariant.
Explain why the impulse response completely characterises an LTI system, and relate it to an instrument or detector response.

lessons.title: Convolution: Superposing Responses and Broadening Lines
objectives: Compute the convolution of short sequences by hand, as a sum of scaled and shifted copies of the impulse response.
Explain line broadening as convolution of a spectrum with an instrument function, including how Gaussian and Lorentzian widths combine.

lessons.title: The DFT: What a Frequency Bin Means
objectives: Describe the DFT as the projection of N samples onto N complex sinusoids, and relate bin index k to frequency k f_s / N.
Explain the conjugate symmetry of the DFT of a real signal (negative frequencies) and the periodic extension assumed by the DFT.

lessons.title: The FFT, Frequency Resolution and Zero-Padding
objectives: Explain that the FFT is an exact fast algorithm for the DFT (about N log2 N operations) and say why that matters.
Show that frequency resolution is set by record length (Δf ≈ 1/T), not by sampling rate or zero-padding.
Describe what zero-padding does (interpolates the spectrum) and does not do (separate unresolved peaks).

lessons.title: Windowing and Spectral Leakage
objectives: Explain spectral leakage as multiplication by a finite window, i.e. convolution of the true spectrum with the window's transform.
Compare windows by main-lobe width and side-lobe level and choose one for a given task.

lessons.title: The Convolution Theorem, FFT Convolution and Deconvolution
objectives: State the convolution theorem and use it to explain why smoothing is multiplication of the spectrum and why FFT convolution is fast.
Explain deconvolution as division in the frequency domain and why it amplifies noise wherever the response is small; describe regularisation (Wiener).

units.title: Digital Filters
units.summary: Smoothing as convolution: moving-average and Savitzky-Golay filters (FIR), recursive RC-style filters (IIR), and a light look at the z-transform with its poles and zeros.

lessons.title: Moving-Average and FIR Filters
objectives: Write a FIR filter as convolution with a finite impulse response, and derive the moving average's frequency response (a sinc-like shape with nulls at multiples of f_s/M).
Explain why white-noise RMS falls by √M but the filter is a poor low-pass, and what linear phase (symmetric taps) buys you: no peak shift, only a delay.

lessons.title: Savitzky–Golay Smoothing and Derivatives
objectives: Describe Savitzky–Golay as a sliding least-squares polynomial fit that reduces to a fixed FIR filter, and compute the 5-point quadratic smoothing result from the coefficients (-3, 12, 17, 12, -3)/35.
Explain why Savitzky–Golay preserves peak height and width better than a moving average of the same window, and when it fails (window wider than the feature).

lessons.title: Recursive (IIR) Filters and the RC Filter
objectives: Write a one-pole recursive low-pass, relate its coefficient to an RC time constant, and compute α from τ and the sampling interval.
Contrast FIR and IIR filters (cost, phase, stability) and recognise an unstable feedback loop.

lessons.title: The z-Transform, Poles and Zeros (Light)
objectives: Write the transfer function H(z) of a simple FIR or IIR filter and read off its poles and zeros; connect |H| on the unit circle to the frequency response.
Explain stability (poles inside the unit circle) and how zeros on the unit circle make notch filters, linking to the Laplace s-plane picture.

units.title: Noise, Detection and Spectroscopic Applications
units.summary: White, shot and 1/f noise, averaging and lock-in detection, then the instrument pipelines a chemist knows: FT-NMR, FT-IR, baseline correction, peak picking and detection limits.

lessons.title: Noise: White, Shot and 1/f
objectives: Distinguish white noise, shot (counting) noise and 1/f noise by their spectra and physical origin, with ICP-MS and spectrometer examples.
Compute SNR for counting data (SNR = √N) and explain why 1/f noise limits how far averaging helps.

lectures.title: 1/F flicker noise

demoIdeas: Generate white and 1/f noise traces and show their spectra on log-log axes; add the running average to compare.

lessons.title: Signal Averaging and Its Limits
objectives: Show that averaging N coherent scans improves SNR by √N and compute the number of scans needed for a target SNR.
Explain when averaging fails: drifting baselines, non-coherent phase, correlated or 1/f noise.
demoIdeas: Accumulate scans of a noisy FID or spectrum: show SNR vs number of scans on a log-log plot with the √N line and a drifting-noise case.

lessons.title: Lock-In (Phase-Sensitive) Detection
objectives: Explain the lock-in principle: multiply by a reference at the modulation frequency and low-pass filter, giving a DC output proportional to the signal amplitude times cos(phase).
Compute the noise-bandwidth reduction for a given time constant, and explain why modulating the signal moves it away from 1/f noise.
Explain why two quadrature outputs give a phase-independent magnitude R = √(X²+Y²).

lessons.title: FT-NMR: FID, Apodisation, Zero-Filling and Phase Correction
objectives: Describe the FID as a sum of decaying complex exponentials and the spectrum as its Fourier transform; relate T2* to Lorentzian linewidth 1/(πT2*).
Explain apodisation (exponential/Gaussian weighting) as a SNR-versus-resolution trade-off, and zero-filling as interpolation only.
Explain zero- and first-order phase correction as removing a constant plus linear-in-frequency phase error to obtain pure absorption lines.

lessons.title: FT-IR: the Interferogram and Its Transform
objectives: Explain the interferogram I(δ) as the cosine transform of the source spectrum, and relate resolution to maximum optical retardation (Δν̃ = 1/δ_max).
Explain how laser fringe sampling sets the Nyquist wavenumber, and why apodisation trades resolution for line shape (sinc ringing).
State the multiplex (Fellgett) advantage and when it applies.

lessons.title: Baseline Correction, Peak Picking and Line-Shape Fitting
objectives: Explain a baseline as a slowly varying component and correct it by fitting polynomials or splines to peak-free regions, noting how it can distort peaks.
Pick peaks robustly: smooth, use derivative zero-crossings or local maxima above a noise-based threshold (S/N ≥ 3), and relate this to a detection limit.
Distinguish deconvolution (undoing instrument blurring) from peak fitting (modelling overlapping lines with Lorentzian/Gaussian/Voigt shapes).
